1.pericope_label: Save me, O God: the waters come in unto the soul, and the enemies who hate without a cause

schools.summary: Augustine reads the psalm from the far side of the church triumphant and warns that felicity is more to be feared than misery, since tribulation bears fruit while ease breeds a perverse security.

Calvin leaves the occasion open between Saul and Absalom but takes the psalm as prophetic of Christ and written in the name of the whole Church, and presses the drowning figure into physiology; Gill makes Christ himself the petitioner from the first word.

Spurgeon hears David and his Son and Lord in the same cry and fears the water inside the vessel more than the sea outside; Henry makes the trouble dangerous only as it reaches the heart, and turns the hatred without cause into a reason for patience rather than for anger.

Clarke dates the psalm to the captivity and assigns it to an inspired Levite speaking for the captives, allowing only the applications to Christ that the New Testament itself makes; Wesley glosses the waters as tribulations and the restoring as done for peace sake.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the inscription and make the sufferer David under persecution by Saul rather than an ideal righteous man; Ellicott treats the sea of troubles as a common figure, defends the strong word for exterminators, and reports a Syriac variant.

debates: Who is the sufferer in this psalm? Gill answers that the petitioner is Christ as man and priest, Spurgeon hears David and his Son and Lord in one cry, Keil and Delitzsch hold to the inscription and make it David persecuted by Saul rather than an ideal righteous man, Calvin leaves the occasion between Saul and Absalom while taking the psalm as prophetic, and Clarke assigns it to an inspired Levite writing in the person of the captives.

How far may the psalm be applied to Christ? Clarke lays down a rule that the portions the New Testament writers apply to our Lord may be applied and others should be handled carefully, and calls the christological reading of the last clause very gratuitous; Gill by contrast makes the whole prayer Christ own from the opening petition.
outliers: Calvin turns the drowning image into physiology, arguing that a man may keep the water out by stopping mouth and nostrils until the need to breathe compels him to draw it in, so that the waters reach the heart.
Augustine holds that what men call felicity is more to be feared than misery, because misery often brings good fruit out of tribulation while felicity corrupts the soul with a perverse security.
themes: the waters that reach the soul
the identity of the sufferer
restraint in reading the psalm of Christ
weariness in unanswered prayer
hatred without cause

5.pericope_label: Thou knowest my foolishness: reproach borne for God, and the zeal that has eaten him up

schools.summary: Spurgeon concedes that David might say these words but not David Lord, unless they refer to the madness men imputed to him.
Gill keeps Christ as the speaker throughout, offering three constructions of the foolishness that leave him sinless, and locates the zeal in the cleansing of the temple.

Clarke denies flatly that the confession of foolishness can be attributed to Christ, reads the psalm through the captives at the gate and the taunts of the Gentiles, and makes the zeal a desire for the divine glory that absorbs all others; Wesley lets the speaker own his sins while holding that the words were directed by the Spirit to represent a greater sufferer.

Ellicott bounds the Messianic application rather than denying it, raises the shame that spreads to the brethren into a principle of churchmanship, and treats the fasting clause as scarcely intelligible without emendation.

debates: Can the confession of foolishness be spoken by Christ? Clarke asks how such words could be attributed to our Lord however they are twisted, Spurgeon allows them to David but not to David Lord except of imputed madness, Ellicott calls the verse fatal to any view of the author as a prophetic mouthpiece rather than an imperfect type, and Wesley lets the speaker confess real sins, while Gill offers three constructions that keep the speaker sinless.

Where does the zeal for the house fall? Gill puts it in the cleansing of the temple and then in the church, Clarke in a desire for the divine glory that has swallowed every other desire, Ellicott in the repair of the temple or rather in its purity and honour while allowing that house might mean congregation, and Wesley in David with a fuller accomplishment beyond him.
outliers: Clarke reconstructs the taunt from outside as a double question, how a pure and holy Being can love such a people, and how God can deal so hardly with those he professes to love, and observes that the reproach seemed to the pious captives to fall upon their God.
Ellicott finds in the fear of shaming the brethren a near approach to true churchmanship, the esprit de corps of the Kingdom of Heaven, which makes a sin more heinous because it may harm others.
themes: a confession that limits the Messianic reading
shame that spreads from one sufferer to many
reproach borne in the cause of religion
zeal for the house of God
mourning turned into a byword

13.pericope_label: But as for me, my prayer is unto thee: the acceptable time, the pit, and the plea of lovingkindness

schools.summary: Henry holds that affliction does not make the time less acceptable, insists that we may be jeered for well-doing but must never be jeered out of it, and keeps the flood and the pit within the mind as the gulf of despair; Spurgeon divides the hour between rejection on earth and acceptance in heaven and warns that an accepted time can glide away.
Gill sets prayer against reviling, reads the flood as the assault of the enemy or the wrath of God, and takes the hidden face and the drawing nigh of the two verses as the cross and what followed it.

Clarke dates the acceptable time to the close of the seventy years foretold by Jeremiah and reads the enemies rage as the panic of captors whose time is short, and works the two words for mercy back to exuberant kindness and a mother affection; Wesley takes the plea as a claim on a promised salvation.

Ellicott rearranges the clauses of the prayer into a time of grace and a faithful help, argues that the sin confessed earlier had not excluded the sufferer from the covenant, and asks whether the pit that shuts its mouth is a figure or the memory of a real atrocity.

debates: What is the acceptable time? Clarke makes it the close of the seventy years of captivity foretold by Jeremiah, Spurgeon a moment rejected by man and accepted in heaven that may be lost if let slip, Henry a time not made less acceptable by affliction, and Ellicott simply a time of grace which proves that the sin confessed earlier had not broken the covenant.

Is the pit that shuts its mouth a figure or a memory? Gill takes the flood for Satan or the wrath of God and Henry takes the pit for the gulf of despair, while Ellicott notes that the word means a well, usually closed by a stone, and asks whether the verse recalls an actual crime.
outliers: Ellicott compares the closing of the well mouth to the crime at Cawnpore, one of the few places in this corpus where a contemporary atrocity is brought to bear on the text.
Henry turns the mockery of fasting and prayer into a rule, that though we may be jeered for well-doing we must never be jeered out of it.
themes: prayer answering reviling
the acceptable time
the flood that flows but does not overflow
the multitude of tender mercies
the hidden face and the drawing nigh

19.pericope_label: Reproach hath broken my heart: the adversaries known to God, and the gall and vinegar

schools.summary: Spurgeon assembles the adversaries by name into a single court scene and holds that reproach literally broke the heart of the sufferer.
Gill takes the three words for shame as the sum of what was done to the sufferer body and name, and leaves the gall as a bitter herb or an animal gall.

Clarke refuses to comment on the appeal at all, judging that anything he added would weaken it, and reads the gall and vinegar as the rations of captivity; Wesley makes the verse metaphorical in David and proper in Christ.
Ellicott corrects the heaviness to sickness, notes that the vocabulary and figures here are favourites of Jeremiah, identifies the gall with the poppy, and asks whether the psalmist was a Nazarite.

debates: What is the gall that was given for meat? Ellicott identifies it with the poppy that grows everywhere in Palestine and treats the familiar rendering as inherited from an older version, while Gill leaves it between a bitter herb and the gall of an animal and Clarke reads it as the deliberately spoiled rations of a prison.

How literally does the verse belong to the sufferer? Wesley holds that it was fulfilled metaphorically in David and properly in Christ, Clarke applies it first to the captives and then to our Lord, Spurgeon reads the whole passage as the passion, and Ellicott asks whether the author may have been a Nazarite or the language merely figurative.
outliers: Clarke breaks off commenting altogether, judging the appeal inimitable and the sentiment incapable of improvement, and says he can devise no comment that would not lessen its effect.
Ellicott draws an argument about the author from a dietary rule, noting that sour wine was forbidden to Nazarites as a luxury and asking whether the psalmist was one.
themes: reproach seen and recorded by God
the adversaries named
a heart broken by slander
gall for meat and vinegar for drink
the reach of the words beyond the psalmist

22.pericope_label: Let their table become a snare: the imprecations and the blotting out of the book of the living

schools.summary: Henry makes the curses prophecies of a destruction accomplished forty years later and expressly exempts those who repented; Spurgeon admits that David and his Lord part company here before allowing a predictive reading, and turns the snared table into a general warning about the provisions of mercy.

Gill denies any private revenge in the speaker and takes the imprecations as inspired prophecies not to be imitated, reads the darkened eyes as judicial blindness, and leaves the book of the living between animal life and a register of saints.

Clarke insists the verbs be read as futures rather than imperatives, offers to render the demand about iniquity as perverseness repaid with perverseness, and keeps the blotting out to a forfeited earthly life; Wesley matches the punishment of the table to the sin of the gall.

Ellicott reads the curses as a human recoil in the terms of the speaker own misery, takes the darkened eyes as signs of terror rather than blindness, and traces the book of the living through three stages of meaning; Keil and Delitzsch mark this verse as the climax at which the wrath of the persecuted man flames up.

debates: Are the imprecations prayers or predictions? Clarke insists they are predictive and should be read as futures rather than imperatives, Gill calls them inspired prophecies rather than private revenge and warns they are not to be imitated, Henry makes them prophecies of a specific destruction while exempting those who repented, and Spurgeon concedes that at this point David and his Lord part company before allowing the predictive reading; Ellicott alone treats them as a natural recoil, the sufferer hurling back curses in the terms of his own misery.

What is the book of the living? Clarke keeps it to the forfeited land of the living and a long life cut off, Gill offers animal life or a catalogue of living saints, and Ellicott derives the image from civil registers and traces its meaning from mere death through exclusion from the covenant to exclusion from the resurrection.
outliers: Ellicott derives the word rendered habitation from a root meaning circle, so that it is better an encampment where tents are pitched in a ring, and compares the derivation of the English word town.
Clarke proposes rendering the petition about iniquity from the sense of perverseness, so that it asks God to act as crookedly toward them in judgment as they dealt crookedly toward him.
themes: imprecation read as prophecy
retribution matched to the offence
the table turned into a snare
blindness as judgment or as terror
erasure from the book of the living

29.pericope_label: But I am poor and sorrowful: the vow of praise and the promise that God will save Zion

schools.summary: Spurgeon marks the point where complaint gives way to thankful song and applies the lifting up to the reader; Henry takes the preference of praise over sacrifice as a plain intimation that the sacrifices of praise instituted by the ceremonial law would end with those of atonement.

Gill reads the poverty literally of the sufferer in his humiliation, uses the vow of song to confirm singing in the churches, and takes Zion as the church and the seed of the servants as a succession of converts.

Clarke reads the reversal in the words themselves, takes the horns and hoofs as gilded ornament on the authority of present eastern practice, holds that the promise about Zion fixes the psalm to the captivity, and repeats his rule of applying to Christ only what the New Testament applies; Wesley keeps a literal and a heavenly inheritance together.
Ellicott glosses the lifting up as removal to safety, reads the horns and hoofs as marks of a clean animal of fit age, and corrects humble to afflicted.

debates: Does the closing promise fix the date of the psalm? Clarke argues that it does, since there was no Zion belonging to the people in the days of Saul, the stronghold having been taken from the Jebusites only after David came to the throne, so that the psalm must belong to the captivity and the rebuilding to the return; Gill and Wesley read Zion as the church and the promise as spiritual, leaving the historical question open.

What do the horns and hoofs mark? Clarke takes them for the gilded parts of a sacrificial victim, mentioned because most conspicuous, and appeals to a practice still followed in the east; Ellicott takes them as marking a clean animal of fit age; Wesley takes them as marking an age at once tender and mature.
outliers: Clarke closes the psalm by professing that he cannot discern what others see so clearly in it relative to gospel matters, while allowing that what evangelists and apostles apply to our Lord may safely be applied.
Henry infers from the preference of a song over an ox that the ceremonial sacrifices of praise were to end along with those of atonement, the calves of our lips replacing the calves of the stall.
themes: the turn from complaint to praise
a song preferred to a sacrifice
the afflicted encouraged by one deliverance
the date fixed by the promise to Zion
an inheritance for the seed of the servants
